citation.title: Combining List Experiment and Direct Question Estimates of Sensitive Behavior Prevalence
citation.venue: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 2, p. 46 (PDF p. 4)] Suppose we have a random sample of $n$ subjects independently drawn from a large population. Let $X_i = 1$ if subject $i$ engages in a sensitive behavior and $X_i = 0$ otherwise. We attempt to measure the behavior $X_i$ using two methods: direct questioning and list experimentation. Our goal is to identify the prevalence of the sensitive behavior in the population, $\mu = \Pr[X_i = 1]$. Let $Y_i$ be the report of subject $i$ to the direct question. We assume that, under direct questioning, subjects may lie and claim that they do not engage in the behavior but will not lie and falsely claim that they do engage in the behavior. [Assumption 1: p. 46] Assumption 1 (Monotonicity). There exist three latent classes of respondents under direct questioning: those who do not engage in the behavior and report truthfully ($X_i = 0$, $Y_i = 0$), subjects who engage and report truthfully ($X_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$), and subjects who engage but report that they do not, i.e., withhold ($X_i = 1$, $Y_i = 0$). [Direct response: p. 46] Let $p = \Pr[Y_i = 1 \mid X_i = 1]$ be the probability of a subject reporting truthfully to the direct question, given that he or she engages in the sensitive behavior. The response of subject $i$ is $Y_i = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } 1 - \mu + \mu(1 - p) \\ 1 & \text{with probability } \mu p. \end{cases}$ [p. 47 (PDF p. 5)] The probability that subject $i$ engages in the behavior, given a negative response, is therefore $\Pr[X_i = 1 \mid Y_i = 0] = \frac{(1 - p)\mu}{1 - \mu p}$. While direct questioning is sufficient to reveal $\Pr[Y_i = 1] = \mu p$, it is not sufficient to identify $\Pr[Y_i = 0 \mid X_i = 1] = 1 - p$. [List experiment: p. 47] Suppose we have a treatment $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$. In the list experiment, treated subjects ($Z_i = 1$) receive a number of control questions and an additional question about the sensitive behavior. We denote the number of items that the subject states are applicable with $V_i$. [Assumption 2: p. 47] Assumption 2 (No Liars and No Design Effects). Reframing Imai’s (2011) formulations, we observe $V_i = W_i + X_i Z_i$, where $W_i$ is the baseline outcome (under control) for subject $i$ for the list experiment. [Assumption 3: p. 47] We further require that the treatment assignment be independent of the actual behavior, direct question, and baseline response. This is a stricter variant of Imai’s (2011) ignorability assumption. Assumption 3 (Treatment Independence). $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$. [Assumption 4: p. 47] To ensure that all target quantities are well defined (and, later, to facilitate inference), we impose the mild regularity condition that all population variances are positive. Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions). $\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = y] > 0$, for $z, y \in \{0, 1\}$, $\mathrm{Var}[Z_i] > 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}[Y_i] > 0$. [Estimators: Section 3, p. 48 (PDF p. 6)] Define the sample means: $\bar Y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i$, $\bar V_{1,0} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i (1 - Y_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i (1 - Y_i)}$ and $\bar V_{0,0} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i (1 - Z_i)(1 - Y_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i)(1 - Y_i)}$. Define an estimator of $\mu$ based on (1), $\hat\mu = \bar Y + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})$. Let $\gamma = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ be the probability of receiving the treatment question in the list experiment. [Standard estimator: p. 49 (PDF p. 7)] $\hat\mu_S = \bar V_1 - \bar V_0$, where $\bar V_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i}$ and $\bar V_0 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i (1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i)}$. [Not printed as assumptions, but used throughout] The paper states the sampling model only as 'a random sample of $n$ subjects independently drawn from a large population'; its proofs treat $(W_i, X_i, Y_i, Z_i)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, as independent and identically distributed, with $Z_i$ part of the draw and $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = \gamma$ (in the application, p. 53 (PDF p. 11): 'All randomizations used Bernoulli random assignment with equal probability 0.5'). $V_i$ is a count of items on a fixed finite list and is therefore bounded; no moment condition is printed. Assumption 1 is used in the form $Y_i \le X_i$ (no subject has $X_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$). The subgroup means are ratios, and the paper assigns them no value when a $(Z, Y)$ cell of the sample is empty (P019-E003). Printed page numbers are PDF page numbers plus 42. Appendices C to F are in the online supplement (author-appendix.pdf, 7 pp.), not in the article PDF.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 3, first sentence, and the same phrase in Section 5.3, with the assumption range corrected
canonical_claim.location: Proposition 3: p. 50 (PDF p. 8). Section 5.3, paragraph on Table 7: p. 56 (PDF p. 14)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement; '1–3' replaces the printed '1–4' in the first sentence, which is Sol's smallest repair and keeps the separate Assumption 4 requirement; everything else is as printed] Proposition 3. Under the null hypothesis that Assumptions 1–3 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence) hold, $\beta = 1$. For large $n$, if Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions) holds, then a two-sided $p$-value is given by $2\Phi\left(\frac{-|\hat\beta - 1|}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta]}}\right)$, where $\Phi(\cdot)$ is the normal CDF. [The same correction in Section 5.3, p. 56] Among the subgroup of respondents who answer “Yes” to the direct question, the list experiment difference-in-means estimate $\beta$ should be equal to 1, under Assumptions 1–3 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence). [Hypotheses of the first sentence, in full] $Y_i \le X_i$ (Assumption 1); $V_i = W_i + X_i Z_i$ (Assumption 2); $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$ (Assumption 3); and $\Pr[Z_i = z, Y_i = 1] > 0$ for $z = 0, 1$, so that the two conditional expectations in $\beta$ are defined (this is implied by Assumption 4 and is the only part of Assumption 4 that the identity uses). [Conclusion] $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = 1$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Placebo Test I: Section 4.1, p. 50 (PDF p. 8)] Define $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$. Consider estimators $\hat\beta = \bar V_{1,1} - \bar V_{0,1}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i Y_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i) Y_i}$. The paper does not write out $\bar V_{1,1}$ and $\bar V_{0,1}$; by analogy with $\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ (p. 48) they are the sample means of $V_i$ among subjects with $(Z_i, Y_i) = (1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$, and $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance (p. 49). [As printed, p. 50] Proposition 3. Under the null hypothesis that Assumptions 1–4 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence) hold, $\beta = 1$. For large $n$, if Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions) holds, then a two-sided $p$-value is given by $2\Phi\left(\frac{-|\hat\beta - 1|}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta]}}\right)$, where $\Phi(\cdot)$ is the normal CDF. [As printed, p. 56] 'Among the subgroup of respondents who answer “Yes” to the direct question, the list experiment difference-in-means estimate $\beta$ should be equal to 1, under Assumptions 1–4 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence).' [Supplement p. 2, Appendix C] 'The placebo test proposed in Section 4 is a joint test of Assumptions 1-3 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence).'
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor: a numbering misprint. The four names in the parentheses are those of Assumptions 1 to 3 (Assumption 2 carries two names) and Assumption 4 is Non-Degenerate Distributions, which the proposition's second sentence invokes separately. The printed implication is not false, since Assumptions 1–4 are a stronger hypothesis than Assumptions 1–3; the validator gave no counterexample. The formal content of this target is the exact first sentence; the second sentence (the large-sample $p$-value) is unchanged by the correction and belongs to the headline target P019-T21. Derivation (the artifact, section 'E001 and N001'): among $Y_i = 1$, Assumption 1 implies $X_i = 1$; Assumption 2 gives control $V_i = W_i$ and treated $V_i = W_i + 1$; Assumption 3 gives the same conditional law of $W_i$ in the two arms. The same identity is correction (e) of P019-T11 and part (ii) of P019-T8; one formal statement serves all three.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A.1, Table A1, row 'CNN (L5 & D5)' (list item 'read or watch' against direct question 'watch'), with the reading in Section 5.2 that the list experiments and the direct questions measure the same quantities
canonical_claim.location: Table A1: p. 61 (PDF p. 19). Section 5.2: p. 54 (PDF p. 12)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [Table A1, Survey Questions and Response Options, row 'CNN (L5 & D5)': p. 61 (PDF p. 19)] List question: 'Here is a list of four (five) news organizations. Please read all four (five) and select how many you read or watch in the course of an ordinary month. We do not want to know which ones, just how many.' Items: The New York Times; CNN; The Huffington Post; Fox News; Politico (CNN is the item in bold, the one added for the treatment list). Direct question: 'In the course of an ordinary month, do you watch CNN?' Response options: Yes; No. [Section 5.2: p. 54 (PDF p. 12)] the estimates generally agree (providing confidence that the list experiments and the direct questions are measuring the same quantities) [What is refuted] That, for the CNN item as worded, the observable responses identify the prevalence of the behavior the direct question asks about (watching), and that a direct 'No' from a respondent who counts CNN on the list is withholding. [Non-identification pair, from the validator] Let $R$ indicate reading CNN and $Q$ watching CNN in an ordinary month, and let $X = \max(R, Q)$ indicate reading or watching, the behavior the list item asks about; a truthful answer to the printed direct question is $Q$. In both worlds $W$ is 1 or 2 with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each, $Z$ is Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$), the respondent type, $W$ and $Z$ are independent, and $V = W + XZ$. World A (every direct answer truthful, $Y = Q$): the types $(R, Q, X, Y)$ are $(0, 1, 1, 1)$ with probability $\frac{1}{4}$, $(1, 0, 1, 0)$ with probability $\frac{1}{4}$ (reads only) and $(0, 0, 0, 0)$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. World B: the same with the reads-only type replaced by $(0, 1, 1, 0)$ with probability $\frac{1}{4}$ (watches and answers 'No'). Then in each world: (a) $Y \le X$, $V = W + XZ$ and $(W, X, Y) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$, so Assumptions 1 to 3 hold with $X$ = reading or watching; (b) Assumption 4 holds: the cells $(Z, Y) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$ have probabilities $\frac{3}{8}, \frac{1}{8}, \frac{3}{8}, \frac{1}{8}$, conditional means of $V$ equal to $\frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2}, \frac{11}{6}, \frac{5}{2}$ and conditional variances $\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{17}{36}, \frac{1}{4}$, with $\mathrm{Var}[Y] = \frac{3}{16}$ and $\mathrm{Var}[Z] = \frac{1}{4}$; (c) $E[Y] = \frac{1}{4}$, the combined functional of equation (1) is $E[Y] + E[1 - Y](E[V \mid Z = 1, Y = 0] - E[V \mid Z = 0, Y = 0]) = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{11}{6} - \frac{3}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}$, the standard list contrast $E[V \mid Z = 1] - E[V \mid Z = 0]$ is $\frac{1}{2}$, $\beta = 1$ and $\delta = 0$. (d) The joint law of the observables $(Z, Y, V)$ is the same in the two worlds: the atoms $(0,0,1)$, $(0,0,2)$, $(0,1,1)$, $(0,1,2)$, $(1,0,1)$, $(1,0,2)$, $(1,0,3)$, $(1,1,2)$, $(1,1,3)$ have probabilities $\frac{3}{16}, \frac{3}{16}, \frac{1}{16}, \frac{1}{16}, \frac{1}{8}, \frac{3}{16}, \frac{1}{16}, \frac{1}{16}, \frac{1}{16}$. (e) The prevalence of watching is $\Pr[Q = 1] = \frac{1}{4}$ in World A and $\frac{1}{2}$ in World B, while $\Pr[X = 1] = \frac{1}{2}$ in both; and $\Pr[Y \ne Q] = 0$ in World A and $\frac{1}{4}$ in World B. Hence $\Pr[Q = 1]$ is not a function of the law of $(Z, Y, V)$; the combined functional equals the prevalence of reading or watching in both worlds and equals the prevalence of watching only in World B; and the class $(X, Y) = (1, 0)$ consists of truthful respondents in World A and of withholders in World B.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Equation (1), $\beta$ and $\delta$ as in Lemma 1 (p. 47, PDF p. 5), Section 4.1 (p. 50, PDF p. 8) and Section 4.2 (p. 51, PDF p. 9): $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$ and $\delta = E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]$. Assumptions 1–4 as in the standing assumptions, with $X_i$ the indicator of the behavior that the list item elicits. In the paper $X_i$ is a single indicator of 'a sensitive behavior' that both instruments measure (p. 46); the instance separates the behavior asked by the list item ($\max(R, Q)$) from the behavior asked by the direct question ($Q$). $W \in \{1, 2\}$ is a valid count among the four control organizations.
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor, of the interpretive kind: the two printed questions differ in behavioral scope for this one of five topics. The pair is a non-identification argument, not a counterexample to Lemma 1 or to any theorem of the paper, which hold for a single indicator $X_i$; the validator records that the table reproduces the questions accurately and that the Section 5.2 parenthetical is tentative, so no printed sentence is false as printed. The instance makes no claim about how many respondents read CNN without watching it, and it does not explain the paper's CNN placebo rejections (in both worlds $\beta = 1$ and $\delta = 0$). The validator's check.py verifies all of it with exact rational arithmetic (check-output.txt, world_a.csv, world_b.csv beside the derivation), and a second validator upheld it. If the target is taken to be watching, $X = Q$, then in World A Assumption 2 fails for treated reads-only respondents: $\Pr[V \ne W + QZ] = \frac{1}{8}$. A further instance in the artifact (near_agreement.csv) has reads-only mass $\frac{1}{100}$: direct mean $\frac{1}{4}$, list and combined functionals $\frac{13}{50}$, so near agreement of the estimates does not show that the two questions measure the same quantity.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The CNN item (Table A1, row 'CNN (L5 & D5)'): what the list and combined estimands are under the printed wording, corrected reading
canonical_claim.location: Table A1: p. 61 (PDF p. 19). Section 5.2: p. 54 (PDF p. 12). Tables 3 and 6, row CNN: pp. 54 and 56 (PDF pp. 12 and 14)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected claim; from Sol's smallest repair: 'Add a CNN-specific qualification: the direct question asks about watching, whereas the list permits reading or watching; comparability and a withholding interpretation cannot be assumed from these texts or from approximate agreement alone. ... If interpreting the existing list and combined result under the ordinary disjunctive reading and valid numerical assumptions, label its target reading-or-watching; retaining watching requires an additional assumption or measurement that excludes or adjusts for reader-only inclusion.'] [Formal content, with every hypothesis] Let $R$ indicate reading CNN and $Q$ watching CNN in an ordinary month, and let $X = \max(R, Q)$. Suppose every respondent answers both instruments truthfully as worded, so that the direct answer is $Y = Q$ and the list response is $V = W + XZ$, with $W$ the baseline count; suppose $(W, R, Q) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$, $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$ and $0 < \Pr[Q = 1] < 1$. Write $b = \Pr[Q = 1]$ and $a = \Pr[R = 1, Q = 0]$. Then (i) $Y \le X$, and Assumptions 1 to 3 hold with $X$ = reading or watching; (ii) $E[V \mid Z = 1, Y = 0] - E[V \mid Z = 0, Y = 0] = \Pr[X = 1 \mid Y = 0] = \frac{a}{1 - b}$; (iii) the combined functional of equation (1) equals $E[Y] + E[1 - Y]\left(E[V \mid Z = 1, Y = 0] - E[V \mid Z = 0, Y = 0]\right) = b + a = \Pr[X = 1]$, the prevalence of reading or watching, and so does the standard list contrast $E[V \mid Z = 1] - E[V \mid Z = 0]$; (iv) the prevalence of watching is $b = E[Y]$, so the combined and list functionals exceed it by exactly $a$, and they equal it if and only if $a = 0$, that is, if no respondent counts CNN on the list from reading alone; (v) $\beta = 1$ and $\delta = 0$, so neither placebo restriction distinguishes $a > 0$ from $a = 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Printed wording: Table A1, p. 61 (PDF p. 19)] List question: 'Here is a list of four (five) news organizations. Please read all four (five) and select how many you read or watch in the course of an ordinary month. We do not want to know which ones, just how many.' Direct question: 'In the course of an ordinary month, do you watch CNN?' [Equation (1): p. 47 (PDF p. 5)] $\mu = E[Y_i] + E[1 - Y_i](E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0])$. $\beta$ and $\delta$ as in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 (pp. 50–51, PDF pp. 8–9).
canonical_claim.note: The formal content is the 'General calculation' of the artifact (section 2) and is Lemma 1 applied with $X$ = reading or watching; it changes no estimate in Tables 3 and 6 and no theorem. It says what the CNN list and combined estimates target under the ordinary disjunctive reading of the list question, namely the broader behavior, and that a watching interpretation needs the further premise $a = 0$, which the paper does not state and the data cannot check. The qualitative parts of the repair (that comparability cannot be assumed from the question texts, and that future surveys should use matched wording) are not formal. The repair's cost is a weaker conclusion about what the CNN result means; the validator establishes no actual reads-only prevalence.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Appendix D and Figure A2, panel 'N= 100' (power of Placebo Test II), corrected
canonical_claim.location: Online supplement (author-appendix.pdf) p. 3 (Appendix D) and p. 4 (Figure A2, first panel); deposited code ACCG_list_placebo_II_power.R, line 31 against lines 62, 93 and 124. The test is Proposition 4, p. 51 (PDF p. 9)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement: supplement pp. 3–4, Appendix D] The power of Placebo Test II to detect violations of Treatment Independence is equivalent to the power of test of a difference in proportions. Following the implementation in R (see accompanying text: Dalgaard 2008, p. 159), the power of the test for N = 100, 200, 500, and 1000 is shown in Figure A2 below. In all panels, the proportion of “Yes” responses in the treatment group is given on the x-axis, and the proportion in the control group is given on the y-axis. [The defect] The panel 'N= 100' was computed by power.prop.test(n=50, p1, p2) with the default strict=FALSE, which counts only the rejection tail in the direction of the true difference; the panels for N = 200, 500 and 1000 were computed with strict=TRUE, which counts both tails of the two-sided test. [Corrected statement; Sol's smallest repair is to add strict=TRUE to the N = 100 call, so that every panel shows normal-approximation planning power for a two-sided 5% test with both rejection tails included. Formal content, from the validator's derivation] Let each group have size $n > 0$, let $p_1, p_2 \in [0, 1]$ with $S = p_1(1 - p_1) + p_2(1 - p_2) > 0$, let $0 < \alpha < 1$ and $c = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2) > 0$, and put $d = |p_1 - p_2|$ and $V = (p_1 + p_2)\left(1 - \frac{p_1 + p_2}{2}\right)$. The normal-approximation power of the two-sided level-$\alpha$ test is $A + B$, where $A = \Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}\,d - c\sqrt{V}}{\sqrt{S}}\right)$ is the probability of rejecting in the direction of the true difference and $B = \Phi\left(\frac{-\sqrt{n}\,d - c\sqrt{V}}{\sqrt{S}}\right) = 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}\,d + c\sqrt{V}}{\sqrt{S}}\right)$ is the probability of rejecting in the opposite direction. The published 'N= 100' panel shows $A$ alone (with $n = 50$ and $\alpha = \frac{1}{20}$). Then: (i) $V - S = \frac{(p_1 - p_2)^2}{2} \ge 0$; (ii) $0 < B \le \frac{\alpha}{2}$, with $B = \frac{\alpha}{2}$ if and only if $p_1 = p_2$; (iii) hence the published panel understates the two-sided power $A + B$ by $B$, which is positive and at most $\frac{\alpha}{2} = 0.025$; (iv) at $n = 50$, $p_1 = p_2 = \frac{1}{2}$, $\alpha = \frac{1}{20}$: $S = V = \frac{1}{2}$, $d = 0$, $A = \Phi(-c) = \frac{1}{40}$ and $A + B = \frac{1}{20}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Placebo Test II: Section 4.2, p. 51 (PDF p. 9)] Define $\delta = E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]$, with $\hat\delta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i} - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i(1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\delta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(Y_i \mid Z_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(Y_i \mid Z_i = 0)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)}$; Proposition 4 gives the two-sided $p$-value $2\Phi\left(\frac{-|\hat\delta|}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\delta]}}\right)$. [Figure A2: supplement p. 4] Four panels titled 'Power of Placebo Test II' with 'N= 100', 'N= 200', 'N= 500', 'N= 1000'; x-axis Pr(Y=1|Z=1), y-axis Pr(Y=1|Z=0). In the formal statement $p_1 = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid Z = 1)$, $p_2 = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid Z = 0)$ and $n = N/2$ is the size of each group. [R routine, from the validator's saved implementation and help text] power.prop.test with sig.level = 0.05 and alternative = 'two.sided' returns $A$ when strict = FALSE (the default) and $A + B$ when strict = TRUE, with the pooled-variance term $V$ in the critical value and the unpooled term $S$ in the standard deviation of the difference. $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function.
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor. The finding is about code: the correction is one argument in one call, and no formula is printed in the supplement. It is a target because the correction changes the formula that the first panel plots and because the rating rests on the bound in (ii) and (iii) ('understates planning power by at most 0.025'). Item (iv) is the validator's exact counterexample to reading the first panel as two-sided power (check_exact.py and check_exact.out beside the derivation); it is an instance of equality in (ii), so there is no separate counterexample target. Proof of (ii) as the validator gives it: $\sqrt{V/S} \ge 1$ by (i) and $\sqrt{n}\,d/\sqrt{S} \ge 0$, so $(\sqrt{n}\,d + c\sqrt{V})/\sqrt{S} \ge c$, with equality if and only if $d = 0$; $\Phi$ is strictly increasing and positive, and $1 - \Phi(c) = \alpha/2$. The statement concerns R's normal approximation only; it is not a claim about exact finite-sample power of the paper's test, which uses an unpooled estimated variance. On the authors' grid the validator finds the red band around 0.80 unchanged by the correction, and no empirical $p$-value in the paper uses this routine.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Appendix C: the simulated design effect (“ceiling effect”) and the 80% power sentence; Figure A1, lower-left panel 'Violated assumption: no design effects'
canonical_claim.location: Online supplement (author-appendix.pdf) p. 2, Appendix C, second paragraph and footnote 1; p. 3, first paragraph and Figure A1. Main-text counterpart: Section 4.1, last paragraph, pp. 50–51 (PDF pp. 8–9)
canonical_claim.statement: [Supplement p. 2, Appendix C, second paragraph] Control list responses were drawn from a binomial distribution with a success probability of 0.4 and four trials. For those units who do meet the assumptions of No False Confessions, No Liars, or No Design Effects, treatment list responses were set equal to the control list response plus one. The treatment list responses for Liars and False Confessors were set equal to their control list responses. The treatment list response for Design Affected subjects was generated as a “ceiling effect”: the control list plus one, except for those with a “4” on the control list; those units’ treatment list response remained equal to 4.$^1$ [Footnote 1] This is one of many possible design effects; the power of our test to detect any particular design effect depends on the manner in which it changes subjects’ treatment list responses. [Supplement p. 3] When approximately 20% of a sample of 800 confessors falsely confess, lie on the treatment list, or change their responses to the non-sensitive items on the treatment list, the placebo test achieves 80% power. [Figure A1, p. 3] Figure A1: Power of Placebo Test I to Detect Violations of Assumptions 1-3; lower-left panel titled 'Violated assumption: no design effects', x-axis 'Proportion of "Design Affected"', y-axis 'Total Number of Admitters'. [Main text, pp. 50–51] We also explore the power of Placebo Test I using a series of Monte Carlo simulations. We vary a number of factors, including the number of subjects answering “Yes” to the direct question, the proportions of false confessors, liars, and the design affected, and the variance of responses to the control list. The placebo test does not always have high power. For example, if 20 percent of 200 subjects responding “Yes” to the direct question are false confessors, the placebo test only has about 30 percent power. But when 20 percent of 800 subjects answering “Yes” are falsely confessing, the test has approximately 80 percent power. In general, the power of the placebo test depends on both the number of subjects answering “Yes” and the proportion of subjects violating the assumptions. These results are presented in Appendix C (please see the supplementary data online). [The printed design-effect mechanism in symbols] Control response $W \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(4, 0.4)$. A subject who meets the assumptions has treatment response $W + 1$. A Design Affected subject has treatment response $\min(W + 1, 4)$: 'the control list plus one, except for those with a “4” on the control list; those units’ treatment list response remained equal to 4'. The power sentence asserts, for this mechanism among others, that the level-0.05 Placebo Test I rejects with probability about 0.80 when $N_{\mathrm{Yes}} = 800$ and the proportion of Design Affected subjects is approximately 0.20.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Placebo Test I: Section 4.1, p. 50 (PDF p. 8)] Define $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$. Consider estimators $\hat\beta = \bar V_{1,1} - \bar V_{0,1}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i Y_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i) Y_i}$. The paper does not write out $\bar V_{1,1}$ and $\bar V_{0,1}$; by analogy with $\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ (p. 48) they are the sample means of $V_i$ among subjects with $(Z_i, Y_i) = (1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$, and $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance (p. 49). [Simulation design: supplement p. 2] 'We vary the following five quantities: the number of subjects who answer “Yes” to the direct question ($N_{\mathrm{Yes}}$, or $\sum_{i=1}^{N} Y_i$) the variability of responses to the non-sensitive list items, the proportion of $N_{\mathrm{Yes}}$ who falsely confess, the proportion of $N_{\mathrm{Yes}}$ who lie when given the treatment list, and the proportion of $N_{\mathrm{Yes}}$ whose responses to the non-sensitive list items change when given the treatment list.' 'On the x-axis of the first three panels, we vary the proportion of those subjects whose response profile violates one of the assumptions: No False Confessions, No Liars, or No Design Effects, respectively. The proportion of units that violate the other two assumptions was fixed at 0.' 'We conducted 1,000 simulations of each combination.' 'No False Confessions' is the supplement's name for Monotonicity (Assumption 1). [Simulator: deposited code, ACCG_list_source.R] Lines 82–86: design_affector(x) returns x + 1 where x != 4 and x where x == 4. Lines 103–106: V0 <- rbinom(N, size=4, prob=baseline_binomial_prob); V1 <- V0 + Ystar*(1-listliar); V1[designaffected==1] <- design_affector(V0[designaffected==1]) + Ystar[designaffected==1]*(1-listliar[designaffected==1]). In the third panel (ACCG_list_placebo_I_power.R) there are no false confessors, no list liars, 200 withholders, 200 innocents and baseline_binomial_prob = 0.4; the affected units are a uniformly drawn subset of floor(N * proportion) of all N subjects, so that with 800 admitters N = 1200 and exactly 240 units, one-fifth, are affected at proportion 0.20; half of the N subjects are treated, drawn uniformly.
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, included because P019-E004 is rated Moderate. The printed power figure is a Monte Carlo estimate (1,000 simulations per grid cell) and cannot be proved or refuted as an exact statement; the mechanism it is attached to is an exact rule. What can be stated formally about the printed mechanism is its population contrast: with a proportion $\rho$ of “Yes” respondents affected independently of $W$ and $Z$, and no false confessors or liars, $\beta = 1 - \rho \Pr[W = 4] = 1 - \frac{16}{625}\rho$, which is $\frac{3109}{3125}$ at $\rho = \frac{1}{5}$ (P019-T1). The finding: the simulator that generated the panel adds the sensitive item after the capped increment, so the panel and the design-effect clause of the 80% sentence describe $V(1) = \min(W + 1, 4) + 1$, not the printed rule (P019-T2). The false-confession and liar clauses of the sentence, the other panels of Figure A1, and the main-text 30 and 80 percent examples are not affected.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma 1, equation (1), and the remark after its proof
canonical_claim.location: Lemma 1: p. 47 (PDF p. 5). Proof and remark: p. 48 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement: Lemma 1. Given Assumptions 1–4 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, Treatment Independence, and Non-Degenerate Distributions), the prevalence may be represented as $\mu = E[Y_i] + E[1 - Y_i]\left(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]\right)$. (1) [Remark after the proof, p. 48] Note that if Assumptions 2–4 hold, but Assumption 1 (Monotonicity) does not hold, then $E[Y_i] + E[1 - Y_i]\left(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]\right) > \mu$, as then $E[X_i \mid Y_i = 1] < 1$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $X_i$, $Y_i$, $Z_i$, $W_i$, $V_i$, $\mu = \Pr[X_i = 1]$ and Assumptions 1–4 as in the standing assumptions (pp. 46–47, PDF pp. 4–5). All expectations are population expectations for a single subject; Assumption 4 makes the conditioning events have positive probability.
canonical_claim.note: An exact population identity; both readers re-derived it and no finding changes it. The proof as printed (p. 48): 'Proof. By Assumptions 2 and 3, $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0] = W_i + \mu - W_i = \mu$. (2) Then, expanding the left-hand side of (2) by marginalizing over $Y_i$, we represent the prevalence of the sensitive behavior as $\mu = E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 1]E[1 - Y_i] + E[V_i \mid Y_i = 1, Z_i = 1]E[Y_i] - (E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 0]E[1 - Y_i] + E[V_i \mid Y_i = 1, Z_i = 0]E[Y_i]) = (E[V_i \mid Y_i = 1, Z_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Y_i = 1, Z_i = 0])E[Y_i] + (E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 0])E[1 - Y_i] = E[X_i \mid Y_i = 1]E[Y_i] + (E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 0])E[1 - Y_i]$. The result follows since $E[X_i \mid Y_i = 1] = 1$ by Assumption 2.' Two slips in it are corrected under P019-T11 ($E[W_i]$ for $W_i$ in (2); Assumption 1 for Assumption 2 in the last sentence). The marginalization over $Y_i$ uses $\Pr[Y_i = y \mid Z_i = z] = \Pr[Y_i = y]$, from Assumption 3. For the remark, 'Assumption 1 does not hold' means that false confessions have positive probability, $\Pr[X_i = 0, Y_i = 1] > 0$; under Assumptions 2–4 the expression then equals $\mu + \Pr[X_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = \mu + E[Y_i](1 - E[X_i \mid Y_i = 1])$ (the size of the excess is the readers' derivation and is not printed).

canonical_claim.location: p. 49 (PDF p. 7); proof in Appendix B.1, p. 63 (PDF p. 21)
canonical_claim.statement: Proposition 1. Given Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions), the asymptotic variance of $\hat\mu$ is characterized by $\operatorname*{plim}_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu] = \frac{(1 - \mu)^2}{1 - \mu p}\,\mu p + (1 - \mu p) \times \left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}\right]$. (3) [The hypothesis printed in the proposition is Assumption 4 only; the sentence that follows it reads 'Under Assumptions 1–4, $\hat\mu$ is root-$n$ consistent and asymptotically normal', and Assumptions 1–3 are maintained from Section 2.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat\mu = \bar Y + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})$, the sample means, $\gamma = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$, $\mu$ and $p$ as in the standing assumptions (pp. 46–48, PDF pp. 4–6). $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu]$ is the variance of $\hat\mu$ over the sampling of $n$ subjects; $\operatorname{plim}$ is applied to the deterministic sequence $n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu]$, so the statement is a limit of that sequence. The paper does not define $\hat\mu$ on samples with an empty $(Z, Y)$ cell, which have positive probability for every $n$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The printed proof (p. 63) rests on: (a) the identity $\hat\mu = 1 + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1)$, display (8); (b) Lemma 2 (p. 48), '$\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ are uncorrelated with $1 - \bar Y$', which holds conditional on both cells being non-empty (P019-T4 (b); P019-T3 (i) for the printed form); (c) the first equality of (9), the product decomposition of the variance, which is exact only in the form $\mathrm{Var}(AB \mid D) = b^2\,\mathrm{Var}(A \mid D) + E[A^2 h \mid D]$ (P019-T4 (c), (d)); (d) $E[1 - \bar Y] = 1 - \mu p$ and $\mathrm{Var}[1 - \bar Y] = \frac{\mu p(1 - \mu p)}{n}$; (e) $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] = \Pr[X_i = 1 \mid Y_i = 0] = \frac{(1 - p)\mu}{1 - \mu p}$ under Assumptions 1–3, so that $E[\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1 \mid D] = -\frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}$; (f) $\mathrm{Var}(\bar V_{z,0} \mid \mathcal{F}) = \mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0] / N_{z0}$ on $D$. Here $N_{z0}$, $D$, $\mathcal{F}$, $A = 1 - \bar Y$, $b$, $h$ and $s_z = \mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0]$ are as defined in P019-T4. An alternative exact route, from the validator (section 6 of the artifact): with $r = \mu p$, $q = 1 - r$, $m_z = E[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0]$, $\delta^* = m_1 - m_0$ and $\psi = (1 - \delta^*)(Y - r) + (1 - Y)\left[\frac{Z}{\gamma}(V - m_1) - \frac{1 - Z}{1 - \gamma}(V - m_0)\right]$, one has $E[\psi] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\psi) = (1 - \delta^*)^2 rq + q\left(\frac{s_1}{\gamma} + \frac{s_0}{1 - \gamma}\right)$, which equals the right-hand side of (3) because $1 - \delta^* = \frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}$; and on $D$, exactly, $\hat\mu - \mu = (1 - \delta^*)(\bar Y - r) + q\,e - (\bar Y - r)\,e$ with $e = (\bar V_{1,0} - m_1) - (\bar V_{0,0} - m_0)$.
canonical_claim.note: Both readers and the validator confirm formula (3) under Assumptions 1–4 (independent influence-function derivations; Monte Carlo at $n = 1000$ gives $n\,\mathrm{Var}$ of 4.10 against 4.08 from (3)). Three points a formal statement must settle. (1) Hypotheses: the proposition names only Assumption 4; this is recorded as a clarity note (P019-E002), not an error, since Assumptions 1–3 are maintained. They are needed: with $X, Y, W, Z$ mutually independent Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$) and $V = W + XZ$, Assumptions 2–4 hold and Assumption 1 fails, the true limit is $\frac{13}{16}$ and the right-hand side of (3) is $\frac{29}{24}$ (the batch artifact, section 'E002'). (2) Definition of $\hat\mu$ on empty cells: with any fixed bounded values there, $n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu]$ converges to the right-hand side of (3) and the limit does not depend on the choice (section 6 of the artifact); without a convention the variance is undefined for every $n$. (3) The finite-sample steps of the printed proof need the corrections of P019-T4 (finding P019-E003, Minor). The sampling model is independent identically distributed draws with bounded $V_i$. In the validator's population (P019-T3) the right-hand side of (3) is $\frac{7}{6}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Unnumbered statement after Proposition 1 (root-n consistency, asymptotic normality, the plug-in variance estimator) and Corollary 1
canonical_claim.statement: [After Proposition 1] Under Assumptions 1–4, $\hat\mu$ is root-$n$ consistent and asymptotically normal, with a consistent estimator of the variance obtained by substituting sample analogues (i.e., sample means and sample variances) for population quantities. Namely, let $n\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu] = \frac{(1 - \hat\mu)^2}{1 - \bar Y}\,\bar Y + (1 - \bar Y) \times \left[\frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0)}{\hat\gamma} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0)}{1 - \hat\gamma}\right]$, where $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance and $\hat\gamma = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i / n$. These properties are sufficient for construction of Wald-type confidence intervals using $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu]$. Corollary 1. If Assumptions 1–4 hold, then confidence intervals constructed as $\hat\mu \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu]}$ will have $\mu$ $100(1 - \alpha)\%$ coverage for $\mu$ for large $n$. [As printed; the $\mu$ before $100(1 - \alpha)\%$ is a stray symbol, deleted in P019-T11 (c).] A proof follows directly from asymptotic normality and Slutsky’s theorem.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat\mu$, $\bar Y$, $\bar V_{1,0}$, $\bar V_{0,0}$ as in the standing assumptions (p. 48, PDF p. 6). $\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0)$ is the sample variance of $V_i$ among subjects with $Z_i = z$, $Y_i = 0$ (the deposited code uses the divisor one less than the cell count). $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ is not defined in the paper; it is the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution. The paper does not define 'root-$n$ consistent', 'asymptotically normal' or 'coverage ... for large $n$'; the natural reading is $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu - \mu) \Rightarrow N(0, \sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2$ the right-hand side of (3), $n\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu] \to_p \sigma^2$, and $\Pr\left(\mu \in \hat\mu \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu]}\right) \to 1 - \alpha$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a) The plug-in identity: $1 - \hat\mu = (1 - \bar Y)\left(1 - (\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})\right)$, so $\frac{(1 - \hat\mu)^2}{1 - \bar Y}\,\bar Y = \bar Y(1 - \bar Y)\left(1 - (\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})\right)^2$ and the printed estimator is the sample analogue of $(1 - \delta^*)^2 rq + q\left(\frac{s_1}{\gamma} + \frac{s_0}{1 - \gamma}\right)$, in the notation of P019-T18. (b) The population identity $\frac{(1 - \mu)^2}{1 - \mu p}\,\mu p = \mu p(1 - \mu p)\left(\frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}\right)^2$ with $1 - \delta^* = \frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}$ under Assumptions 1–3. (c) The exact decomposition of $\hat\mu - \mu$ and the variance of the influence function $\psi$, as in P019-T18. (d) Positivity of the limit: under Assumption 4 the right-hand side of (3) is strictly positive, which the Wald interval needs.
canonical_claim.note: No proof is printed beyond 'A proof follows directly from asymptotic normality and Slutsky’s theorem', and asymptotic normality itself is asserted, not proved, in the paper. The validator's derivation (section 6 of the artifact) proves the three natural-reading statements for independent identically distributed draws with bounded $V_i$, after fixed bounded values are assigned to the subgroup means on empty cells and to the plug-in variance wherever its formula is undefined (cells with fewer than two observations, zero denominators); such samples have exponentially small probability. A formal statement needs those conventions made explicit; they are the validator's and are not printed. A reader's simulation at $n = 1000$ gives 95% Wald coverage of 0.9495. Nothing printed claims exact finite-sample coverage. The central limit theorem and Slutsky's theorem are the classical inputs.

canonical_claim.location: p. 49 (PDF p. 7); proof in Appendix B.1, pp. 64–65 (PDF pp. 22–23), ending at display (10)
canonical_claim.statement: Proposition 2. Under Assumptions 1–4 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, Treatment Independence, and Non-Degenerate Distributions), $\operatorname*{plim}_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu] < \operatorname*{plim}_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_S]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat\mu$ and its limit (3) as in P019-T18. [Standard estimator: p. 49 (PDF p. 7)] Consider the standard difference-in-means-based estimator for the list experiment, $\hat\mu_S = \bar V_1 - \bar V_0$, where $\bar V_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i}$ and $\bar V_0 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i(1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)}$. [Asymptotic variance of $\hat\mu_S$, first display of the proof, p. 64 (PDF p. 22)] $\operatorname*{plim}_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_S] = (1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}\right] + \mu p\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]}{1 - \gamma}\right] + (1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1])^2}{\gamma}\right] + (1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0])^2}{1 - \gamma}\right] + \mu p\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1])^2}{\gamma}\right] + \mu p\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0])^2}{1 - \gamma}\right]$, which is $\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}$ with each arm's variance decomposed over $Y_i$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The comparison of the two limits is an exact inequality between population quantities; the printed proof (pp. 64–65) uses: (a) the law of total variance over $Y_i$ within each arm, with $\Pr[Y_i = 1 \mid Z_i = z] = \mu p$; (b) the between-group identity that turns the four squared-deviation terms into $\mu p(1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1])^2}{\gamma}\right] + \mu p(1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1])^2}{1 - \gamma}\right]$; (c) $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] + 1$ (printed with 'By Assumptions 1 and 2'; it needs Assumptions 1–3, P019-T11 (e)) and $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] = \frac{(1 - p)\mu}{1 - \mu p}$, which give the third term $\mu p(1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{((\mu - 1)/(1 - \mu p) + E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1])^2}{\gamma}\right]$; (d) the first-order condition: over real $x = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$, the function $\frac{(\kappa + x)^2}{\gamma} + \frac{x^2}{1 - \gamma}$ with $\kappa = \frac{\mu - 1}{1 - \mu p}$ is minimized at $x = [\gamma - 1]\kappa$ with minimum value $\kappa^2$; (e) display (10): $\operatorname{plim} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_S] \ge (1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}\right] + \mu p\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]}{1 - \gamma}\right] + \mu p(1 - \mu p)\left(\frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}\right)^2 \ge \operatorname{plim} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu]$; (f) strictness: 'Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions) ensures that the inequality holds strictly', since $\mu p > 0$ and the two conditional variances given $Y_i = 1$ are positive. In closed form (the validator, section 7 of the artifact; both readers obtain the same): with $r = \mu p$, $q = 1 - r$, $\tau^2 = \mathrm{Var}[W_i \mid Y_i = 1]$, $u = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]$ and $c = \frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}$, the difference of the two limits is $\frac{r\tau^2}{\gamma(1 - \gamma)} + \frac{rq\,[u + (1 - \gamma)c]^2}{\gamma(1 - \gamma)} > 0$.
canonical_claim.note: Held up for both readers; every algebraic step of the printed proof was re-derived and the gap verified symbolically and on exact cases (in the validator's population of P019-T3 the limits are $\frac{7}{6}$ and $\frac{3}{2}$, gap $\frac{1}{3}$). The asymptotic content is the two limits: that of $\hat\mu$ is Proposition 1 (P019-T18), and that of $\hat\mu_S$ is stated at the start of the proof without derivation (it is the first-order variance of a difference of two ratio means; exact finite-sample variances of both estimators are undefined without a convention for empty groups). The exact content is the strict inequality between the right-hand side of (3) and $\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}$ under Assumptions 1–4. The only slip in the proof is the assumption citation in step (c), finding P019-E008 (Minor).

canonical_claim.statement: Proposition 3. Under the null hypothesis that Assumptions 1–4 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence) hold, $\beta = 1$. For large $n$, if Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions) holds, then a two-sided $p$-value is given by $2\Phi\left(\frac{-|\hat\beta - 1|}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta]}}\right)$, where $\Phi(\cdot)$ is the normal CDF. [Following sentence, p. 50] A proof for Proposition 3 follows directly from calculations analogous to those for Proposition 1.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Placebo Test I: Section 4.1, p. 50 (PDF p. 8)] Define $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$. Consider estimators $\hat\beta = \bar V_{1,1} - \bar V_{0,1}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i Y_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i) Y_i}$. The paper does not write out $\bar V_{1,1}$ and $\bar V_{0,1}$; by analogy with $\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ (p. 48) they are the sample means of $V_i$ among subjects with $(Z_i, Y_i) = (1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$, and $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance (p. 49). [Preceding text, p. 50] It is possible to jointly test the Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence assumptions. Under these assumptions, for all $t$, $\Pr[V_i = t \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = \Pr[V_i = (t + 1) \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]$, thus tests of distributional equality are appropriate. ... However, since distributional equality implies that $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = 1$, a simple test is available. The paper does not define 'a two-sided $p$-value ... for large $n$'; the natural reading is that under the null $(\hat\beta - 1)/\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta]} \Rightarrow N(0, 1)$, so that the displayed quantity is asymptotically uniform on $(0, 1)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a) The first sentence is exact: under Assumptions 1–3 and $\Pr[Z_i = z, Y_i = 1] > 0$ for $z = 0, 1$, $\beta = 1$ (P019-T12; as printed the hypothesis is Assumptions 1–4, which is stronger). (b) Under the same hypotheses the conditional law of $V_i$ given $Z_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$ equals that of $V_i - 1$ given $Z_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$ (P019-T6). (c) For the large-sample sentence: the exact ratio identity $\hat m - m = \frac{n^{-1}\sum_i I_i(V_i - m)}{n^{-1}\sum_i I_i}$ for each of the two cell means, and the influence function $\psi = \frac{Y_iZ_i}{q\gamma}(V_i - m - 1) - \frac{Y_i(1 - Z_i)}{q(1 - \gamma)}(V_i - m)$ with $q = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$ and $m = E[W_i \mid Y_i = 1]$, whose variance is $\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]}{q\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]}{q(1 - \gamma)}$, the limit of $n\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta]$. (d) For $G$ standard normal and $0 < u < 1$, $\Pr(2\Phi(-|G|) \le u) = u$.
canonical_claim.note: Held up for both readers: $\beta = 1$ under the stated null, and the variance estimator and the two-sided $p$-value formula (with the minus sign) are as the code implements them. The range 'Assumptions 1–4' in the first sentence is a numbering misprint for 1–3 (P019-N001, Minor; corrected statement P019-T12); the printed sentence is true as it stands because its hypothesis is stronger. The paper gives no proof of the large-sample sentence beyond the analogy with Proposition 1; the influence-function expansion in (c) is the validator's (the P019-N003 artifact, section 1) and needs independent identically distributed draws, bounded $V_i$, and a convention for samples in which a $(Z, Y = 1)$ cell has fewer than two subjects. Passing the test does not establish the assumptions, as the paper says; the converse reading in the supplement is the subject of P019-T7 and P019-T8.

canonical_claim.statement: Proposition 4. Under the null hypothesis that Assumption 3 holds, $\delta = 0$. For large $n$, if Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions) holds, then a two-sided $p$-value is given by $2\Phi\left(\frac{-|\hat\delta|}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\delta]}}\right)$. [Following sentences, p. 51] A proof for Proposition 4 again follows directly from calculations analogous to those for Proposition 1. When the treatment is randomly assigned, Placebo Test II is simply a test of whether $Z_i$ has a causal effect on $Y_i$. When $Z_i$ is randomly assigned and the list experiment treatment is presented after the direct question, Assumption 3 holds by design.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Section 4.2, p. 51 (PDF p. 9)] We can probe the validity of the Treatment Independence assumption with a second placebo test. Treatment Independence is violated if the answer to the direct question is systematically related to treatment assignment (i.e., $Y_i \not\perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$). Define $\delta = E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]$. Consider the estimators $\hat\delta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i} - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i(1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\delta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(Y_i \mid Z_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(Y_i \mid Z_i = 0)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)}$. Assumption 3 is $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$ (p. 47, PDF p. 5); $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance and $\Phi(\cdot)$ the normal CDF (pp. 49–50). The natural reading of the second sentence is that under the null $\hat\delta/\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\delta]} \Rightarrow N(0, 1)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a) The first sentence is exact: if $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$ and $0 < \Pr[Z_i = 1] < 1$, then $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$, so $E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] = E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0] = E[Y_i]$ and $\delta = 0$. (b) Because $Y_i$ is binary, $\delta = 0$ is equivalent to $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$; it does not imply Assumption 3 (the instances of P019-T7 have $\delta = 0$ with Assumption 3 false). (c) For the large-sample sentence: the first-order variance of $\hat\delta$ is $\frac{\mathrm{Var}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1]}{n\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{n(1 - \gamma)}$, and for $G$ standard normal and $0 < u < 1$, $\Pr(2\Phi(-|G|) \le u) = u$.
canonical_claim.note: Held up for both readers; no finding changes the proposition. Findings near it concern labels and a figure, not the statement: the Placebo Test II tables head the estimate column $\hat\beta$ where $\hat\delta$ is meant (P019-E009, not a formalization target), and the first panel of the supplement's power figure for this test omits one rejection tail (P019-T15). Assumption 4 gives $\mathrm{Var}[Y_i] > 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}[Z_i] > 0$, hence $0 < \Pr[Y_i = 1 \mid Z_i = z] < 1$ under the null, which the normal limit needs. The paper gives no proof of the large-sample sentence beyond the analogy with Proposition 1.
